frames.heading: Two ways for a cell to die

lines.say: Cells don't live forever, and that is often a good thing.
Apoptosis is programmed cell death. The cell does it itself, using ATP.
Necrosis is uncontrolled death after severe injury, like losing blood supply.
Watch the apoptotic cell. It shrinks and packs itself into apoptotic bodies.

draw.alt: Apoptotic cell shrinking into small apoptotic bodies

lines.say: The necrotic cell swells, the membrane bursts, and the contents spill out.

draw.alt: Necrotic cell swelling and bursting, contents spilling

lines.say: Apoptotic cells flip phosphatidylserine to the outside of the membrane.
That is an eat me signal. Macrophages swallow the bodies before anything leaks.
In necrosis, the spilled contents trigger inflammation and damage nearby tissue.
Apoptosis usually takes single cells. Necrosis often takes groups of cells.
A heart attack causes necrosis. Sunburnt skin cells are removed by apoptosis.
Before birth, cells between your fingers died on cue. That's apoptosis.
The immune system removes T cells that would attack your own tissues.
It also balances cell division, so organs stay the right size.
And it removes cells with DNA damage that can't be repaired.
Caspases are protease enzymes. They start as inactive procaspases.
Extrinsic pathway: Fas ligand binds a death receptor. That switches on caspase 8.
Intrinsic pathway: stress tips the Bcl-2 family balance towards Bax and Bak.
Cytochrome c leaks out, joins Apaf-1 to make the apoptosome, and activates caspase 9.
Both pathways meet at executioner caspase 3. Each step amplifies the signal.

draw.alt: Extrinsic and intrinsic pathways converging on caspase-3

lines.say: Caspase 3 cuts the cytoskeleton, the nuclear lamina, and DNA. There's no going back.
Telomeres are repeats of T T A G G G at the chromosome ends.
DNA polymerase can't fill the last gap on the lagging strand. That's the end replication problem.
So each division, the telomere gets a bit shorter.
Critically short telomeres look like DNA damage. p53 stops the cell for good.
Senescent cells are alive. They have just permanently stopped dividing.
Telomerase adds repeats back. It's active in germ-line, stem and cancer cells.
Ageing has several overlapping causes, not just one.
Telomere loss, free radical damage, mutation build-up, genes, and evolution all play a part.
Cancer is uncontrolled division. Think of an accelerator and brakes.

draw.alt: Oncogene as stuck accelerator, tumour suppressor as brakes

lines.say: A mutated proto-oncogene becomes an oncogene. One copy is enough.
Tumour suppressors like T P 53 need both copies lost. That's the two hit hypothesis.
Cancer cells also evade apoptosis and switch telomerase back on.
Apoptosis isn't always harmful. It's essential for development and stopping cancer.
Necrosis does not need energy. Apoptosis is the one that needs ATP.
Don't call senescent cells dead. They're alive but stopped dividing.
Telomerase isn't active in all cells. Mostly germ-line, stem and cancer cells.
Apoptosis: shrink and pack. Necrosis: swell and burst.
Eight from outside, nine from inside, both meet at three.
Telomeres shorten each division until the cell becomes senescent.
Oncogene is a stuck accelerator. Tumour suppressor is the brakes.
